Low detail is the goal, not a side effect: the brush is too broad to paint anything fine, so every form is built from a few large strokes and flat color shapes. Take only the main subject's identity, silhouette and major structure from the reference; discard all of its photographic texture and small detail, and repaint the whole scene from scratch in this broad-brush language.

Input image: reference for the main subject's identity, silhouette and major structure only; not a fixed composition and not a source of detail.
Primary request: Repaint the reference granary as a monumental historical painting. Keep the visible grey-brick granary buildings, roof pitches, roof relationships and doorway proportions recognizable. Remove the glass office blocks and museum fixtures. A slightly lower, closer viewpoint, a reorganized earthen or stone courtyard, a few small grain porters, sacks or a wooden handcart may give these solid storehouses weight and purpose. Do not replicate the building into an immense warehouse city or add a canal or imperial palace.

Composition/framing: preserve the subject's identity, defining silhouette, structural relationships and believable proportions. You may modestly change camera height, distance or angle within the same recognizable view and bring the subject forward in the composition. Simplify, remove or merge secondary vegetation, paths, clouds and haze; add at most a few small figures or objects, and only where they help scale. Fewer, larger shapes are always better than many small ones: remove clutter rather than repainting it. Keep the main subject complete, dominant and readable at thumbnail size, with space around its highest and lowest features. Favor horizontal framing when the source supports it; its aspect ratio and empty areas are not locked.

Style/medium: coarse-brush oil paint with the clear shape design of a hand-painted cartoon background. Imagine a small canvas and a wide flat brush: the smallest mark anywhere in the picture is one visible brushstroke about 1/80 of the image width, so nothing finer can exist. Build buildings, trees, ground, water and sky from large flat or softly graded color shapes, each finished with only a few loose, visible strokes. Spend the little detail there is on the main subject's silhouette and its major divisions (towers, domes, roof lines, big arches, column groups); inside any shape allow only two or three strokes of variation.
How to paint each element: trees and forests are a few rounded masses in two or three greens, light on top and dark below, with a handful of dabs along the edge; no individual leaves or twigs, only a few main trunks. Grass, fields and slopes are broad planes of color with a few long directional strokes; no grass blades, flowers or pebbles. Rock, scree, rubble and masonry are large faceted planes; stones and bricks are never drawn one by one. Water is flat bands of color with a few horizontal highlight strokes, no ripple or wave pattern. Clouds are two to four big soft shapes. Windows, tiles, carving, tilework, frescoes and ornament are implied by a short rhythm of dark or light dabs or a single tone change, never drawn unit by unit. People are one- or two-stroke silhouettes with a dab for the head, without faces, hands or costume detail; a group merges into one shape. Ships' rigging is a few strokes, not every rope.
Light and color: three or four clear value masses (light, midtone, shadow, one warm accent on the main subject) with designed shadow shapes. Earthy but distinct palette of ochre, terracotta, muted greens and slate-blue shadows. Selective dark warm contours only on the main silhouette and key structural edges, with varied weight; distant forms have soft lost edges and no outline. Keep material weight, solemn grandeur and believable architectural proportions.
Avoid: fine texture, photographic, engraved or illustrated microdetail, hair-thin lines, crisp ornament, individually painted leaves, grass, flowers, bricks, stones, waves, ropes or faces, dense crowds, smooth airbrushed photorealism, glossy 3D rendering, cinematic concept-art polish, uniform heavy comic outlines, childish proportions and an all-over sepia or canvas-texture filter. The coarse oil-paint character must come from how every form is painted, not from a texture overlay.

Constraints: supporting additions must suit the setting and remain subordinate. Remove modern visitors, vehicles, signs, electric fixtures and tourist equipment. Keep the monument's own geometry coherent when changing viewpoint; do not physically stretch it, multiply its structures, or invent major wings, towers or famous landmarks to manufacture grandeur. No added readable text, logo, watermark or UI.
Final check: shrunk to a 200-pixel thumbnail, the picture must read as a bold, coarse-brush painting. If any area looks finely rendered (foliage, grass, crowds, masonry, water, ornament), repaint it as a few broad strokes.

Low detail is the goal, not a side effect: the brush is too broad to paint anything fine, so every form is built from a few large strokes and flat color shapes. Take only the main subject's identity, silhouette and major structure from the reference; discard all of its photographic texture and small detail, and repaint the whole scene from scratch in this broad-brush language.

Input image: reference for the main subject's identity, silhouette and major structure only; not a fixed composition and not a source of detail.
Primary request: Repaint the reference Baku fire temple. Preserve the central stone fire pavilion, its roof and openings, the flame's credible scale and the enclosing courtyard relationship. A slightly lower viewpoint, heavy weathered stone, warm firelight against cool dusk and a few tiny period worshippers can emphasize its sacred presence. You may reorganize ground textures and the peripheral atmosphere; do not add temples, duplicate altars or turn the flame into a colossal supernatural blaze.

Composition/framing: preserve the subject's identity, defining silhouette, structural relationships and believable proportions. You may modestly change camera height, distance or angle within the same recognizable view and bring the subject forward in the composition. Simplify, remove or merge secondary vegetation, paths, clouds and haze; add at most a few small figures or objects, and only where they help scale. Fewer, larger shapes are always better than many small ones: remove clutter rather than repainting it. Keep the main subject complete, dominant and readable at thumbnail size, with space around its highest and lowest features. Favor horizontal framing when the source supports it; its aspect ratio and empty areas are not locked.

Style/medium: coarse-brush oil paint with the clear shape design of a hand-painted cartoon background. Imagine a small canvas and a wide flat brush: the smallest mark anywhere in the picture is one visible brushstroke about 1/80 of the image width, so nothing finer can exist. Build buildings, trees, ground, water and sky from large flat or softly graded color shapes, each finished with only a few loose, visible strokes. Spend the little detail there is on the main subject's silhouette and its major divisions (towers, domes, roof lines, big arches, column groups); inside any shape allow only two or three strokes of variation.
How to paint each element: trees and forests are a few rounded masses in two or three greens, light on top and dark below, with a handful of dabs along the edge; no individual leaves or twigs, only a few main trunks. Grass, fields and slopes are broad planes of color with a few long directional strokes; no grass blades, flowers or pebbles. Rock, scree, rubble and masonry are large faceted planes; stones and bricks are never drawn one by one. Water is flat bands of color with a few horizontal highlight strokes, no ripple or wave pattern. Clouds are two to four big soft shapes. Windows, tiles, carving, tilework, frescoes and ornament are implied by a short rhythm of dark or light dabs or a single tone change, never drawn unit by unit. People are one- or two-stroke silhouettes with a dab for the head, without faces, hands or costume detail; a group merges into one shape. Ships' rigging is a few strokes, not every rope.
Light and color: three or four clear value masses (light, midtone, shadow, one warm accent on the main subject) with designed shadow shapes. Earthy but distinct palette of ochre, terracotta, muted greens and slate-blue shadows. Selective dark warm contours only on the main silhouette and key structural edges, with varied weight; distant forms have soft lost edges and no outline. Keep material weight, solemn grandeur and believable architectural proportions.
Avoid: fine texture, photographic, engraved or illustrated microdetail, hair-thin lines, crisp ornament, individually painted leaves, grass, flowers, bricks, stones, waves, ropes or faces, dense crowds, smooth airbrushed photorealism, glossy 3D rendering, cinematic concept-art polish, uniform heavy comic outlines, childish proportions and an all-over sepia or canvas-texture filter. The coarse oil-paint character must come from how every form is painted, not from a texture overlay.

Constraints: supporting additions must suit the setting and remain subordinate. Remove modern visitors, vehicles, signs, electric fixtures and tourist equipment. Keep the monument's own geometry coherent when changing viewpoint; do not physically stretch it, multiply its structures, or invent major wings, towers or famous landmarks to manufacture grandeur. No added readable text, logo, watermark or UI.
Final check: shrunk to a 200-pixel thumbnail, the picture must read as a bold, coarse-brush painting. If any area looks finely rendered (foliage, grass, crowds, masonry, water, ornament), repaint it as a few broad strokes.

Low detail is the goal, not a side effect: the brush is too broad to paint anything fine, so every form is built from a few large strokes and flat color shapes. Take only the main subject's identity, silhouette and major structure from the reference; discard all of its photographic texture and small detail, and repaint the whole scene from scratch in this broad-brush language.

Primary request: Repaint the reference Monks Mound at Cahokia. Keep the broad flat-topped earthen mound with its terraces, the long low profile across the plain, the stair line up its front and the single tree on the left. Paint the mound as two or three big green planes with a light top and a shaded flank, the plain as one broad yellow-green plane with a few long strokes and the sky as two soft clouds. Replace the modern stairs with a simple earthen ramp. Two or three small figures may stand on the plain. Do not add palisades, a woodhenge, a town or temples on top; the reference shows the mound only.

Composition/framing: preserve the subject's identity, defining silhouette, structural relationships and believable proportions. You may modestly change camera height, distance or angle within the same recognizable view and bring the subject forward in the composition. Simplify, remove or merge secondary vegetation, paths, clouds and haze; add at most a few small figures or objects, and only where they help scale. Fewer, larger shapes are always better than many small ones: remove clutter rather than repainting it. Keep the main subject complete, dominant and readable at thumbnail size, with space around its highest and lowest features. Favor horizontal framing when the source supports it; its aspect ratio and empty areas are not locked.

Style/medium: coarse-brush oil paint with the clear shape design of a hand-painted cartoon background. Imagine a small canvas and a wide flat brush: the smallest mark anywhere in the picture is one visible brushstroke about 1/80 of the image width, so nothing finer can exist. Build buildings, trees, ground, water and sky from large flat or softly graded color shapes, each finished with only a few loose, visible strokes. Spend the little detail there is on the main subject's silhouette and its major divisions (towers, domes, roof lines, big arches, column groups); inside any shape allow only two or three strokes of variation.
How to paint each element: trees and forests are a few rounded masses in two or three greens, light on top and dark below, with a handful of dabs along the edge; no individual leaves or twigs, only a few main trunks. Grass, fields and slopes are broad planes of color with a few long directional strokes; no grass blades, flowers or pebbles. Rock, scree, rubble and masonry are large faceted planes; stones and bricks are never drawn one by one. Water is flat bands of color with a few horizontal highlight strokes, no ripple or wave pattern. Clouds are two to four big soft shapes. Windows, tiles, carving, tilework, frescoes and ornament are implied by a short rhythm of dark or light dabs or a single tone change, never drawn unit by unit. People are one- or two-stroke silhouettes with a dab for the head, without faces, hands or costume detail; a group merges into one shape. Ships' rigging is a few strokes, not every rope.
Light and color: three or four clear value masses (light, midtone, shadow, one warm accent on the main subject) with designed shadow shapes. Earthy but distinct palette of ochre, terracotta, muted greens and slate-blue shadows. Selective dark warm contours only on the main silhouette and key structural edges, with varied weight; distant forms have soft lost edges and no outline. Keep material weight, solemn grandeur and believable architectural proportions.
Avoid: fine texture, photographic, engraved or illustrated microdetail, hair-thin lines, crisp ornament, individually painted leaves, grass, flowers, bricks, stones, waves, ropes or faces, dense crowds, smooth airbrushed photorealism, glossy 3D rendering, cinematic concept-art polish, uniform heavy comic outlines, childish proportions and an all-over sepia or canvas-texture filter. The coarse oil-paint character must come from how every form is painted, not from a texture overlay.

Constraints: supporting additions must suit the setting and remain subordinate. Remove modern visitors, vehicles, signs, electric fixtures and tourist equipment. Keep the monument's own geometry coherent when changing viewpoint; do not physically stretch it, multiply its structures, or invent major wings, towers or famous landmarks to manufacture grandeur. No added readable text, logo, watermark or UI.
Final check: shrunk to a 200-pixel thumbnail, the picture must read as a bold, coarse-brush painting. If any area looks finely rendered (foliage, grass, crowds, masonry, water, ornament), repaint it as a few broad strokes.

Primary request: Repaint the reference William Alexander watercolor of the South Gate of Tinghai (Dinghai) on Zhoushan, drawn in 1793. Keep the gate tower with its two-tier roof over the city wall, the tall pagoda-like watchtower behind it, the smaller roofed buildings, the crenellated wall and the porter in front. Paint the walls as broad grey planes with a notched top, the roofs as dark grey shapes with light edges and the watchtower as a pale stacked shape. Fill the empty background with a soft hilly island skyline and sea. The reference shows a city gate, not beacons: do not invent a chain of signal fires across islands.

You may modestly change camera height, distance or angle within the same recognizable view and bring the subject forward in the composition. Simplify, remove or merge secondary vegetation, paths, clouds and haze; add at most a few small figures or objects, and only where they help scale. Fewer, larger shapes are always better than many small ones: remove clutter rather than repainting it. Keep the main subject complete, dominant and readable at thumbnail size, with space around its highest and lowest features. Favor horizontal framing when the source supports it; its aspect ratio and empty areas are not locked.

Style/medium: coarse-brush oil paint with the clear shape design of a hand-painted cartoon background. Imagine a small canvas and a wide flat brush: the smallest mark anywhere in the picture is one visible brushstroke about 1/80 of the image width, so nothing finer can exist. Build buildings, trees, ground, water and sky from large flat or softly graded color shapes, each finished with only a few loose, visible strokes. Spend the little detail there is on the main subject's silhouette and its major divisions (towers, domes, roof lines, big arches, column groups); inside any shape allow only two or three strokes of variation.
How to paint each element: trees and forests are a few rounded masses in two or three greens, light on top and dark below, with a handful of dabs along the edge; no individual leaves or twigs, only a few main trunks. Grass, fields and slopes are broad planes of color with a few long directional strokes; no grass blades, flowers or pebbles. Rock, scree, rubble and masonry are large faceted planes; stones and bricks are never drawn one by one. Water is flat bands of color with a few horizontal highlight strokes, no ripple or wave pattern. Clouds are two to four big soft shapes. Windows, tiles, carving, tilework, frescoes and ornament are implied by a short rhythm of dark or light dabs or a single tone change, never drawn unit by unit. People are one- or two-stroke silhouettes with a dab for the head, without faces, hands or costume detail; a group merges into one shape. Ships' rigging is a few strokes, not every rope.
Light and color: three or four clear value masses (light, midtone, shadow, one warm accent on the main subject) with designed shadow shapes. Earthy but distinct palette of ochre, terracotta, muted greens and slate-blue shadows. Selective dark warm contours only on the main silhouette and key structural edges, with varied weight; distant forms have soft lost edges and no outline. Keep material weight, solemn grandeur and believable architectural proportions.
Avoid: fine texture, photographic, engraved or illustrated microdetail, hair-thin lines, crisp ornament, individually painted leaves, grass, flowers, bricks, stones, waves, ropes or faces, dense crowds, smooth airbrushed photorealism, glossy 3D rendering, cinematic concept-art polish, uniform heavy comic outlines, childish proportions and an all-over sepia or canvas-texture filter. The coarse oil-paint character must come from how every form is painted, not from a texture overlay.

Constraints: supporting additions must suit the setting and remain subordinate. Remove modern visitors, vehicles, signs, electric fixtures and tourist equipment. Keep the monument's own geometry coherent when changing viewpoint; do not physically stretch it, multiply its structures, or invent major wings, towers or famous landmarks to manufacture grandeur. No added readable text, logo, watermark or UI.
Final check: shrunk to a 200-pixel thumbnail, the picture must read as a bold, coarse-brush painting. If any area looks finely rendered (foliage, grass, crowds, masonry, water, ornament), repaint it as a few broad strokes.
